CausalChain: Tumor cells exhibit high glycolytic activity -> Increased lactate secretion into the tumor microenvironment -> Uptake of lactate by MDSCs -> Lactate induces histone lactylation in MDSCs -> Upregulation of immunosuppressive genes (e.g., ARG1, iNOS) -> Enhanced T cell suppression (in parallel with GM‑CSF/STAT3 signaling) -> Tumor progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that tumor-derived lactate not only reinforces immune suppression through its effects on T regulatory cells but also, when taken up by MDSCs, induces selective histone lactylation that upregulates key immunosuppressive genes. This lactate-mediated epigenetic reprogramming acts in concert with the established GM‑CSF/STAT3 signaling pathway to amplify MDSC-mediated T cell suppression and promote tumor progression. By concurrently targeting lactate production/transport and lactylation (using chemical inhibitors or CRISPR-based strategies) along with inhibition of the GM‑CSF/STAT3 axis, it is expected that the immunosuppressive TME can be effectively disrupted, thereby restoring antitumor immunity. Cutting-edge methods such as single-cell RNA and epigenomic sequencing, multiplex CRISPR screens, and in vivo lactate imaging will be pivotal for delineating mechanistic details and optimizing translational therapeutic interventions.
Abstract: Tumor cells exhibit high glycolytic activity that produces an abundance of lactate, which not only contributes to the known stabilization of regulatory T cells but also plays a critical role in reprogramming myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). In our revised model, tumor‐derived lactate is internalized by MDSCs where it induces specific histone lactylation at regulatory regions of immunosuppressive genes, including ARG1 and iNOS. This epigenetic modification integrates with the canonical GM‑CSF/STAT3 signaling pathway to synergistically enhance the immunosuppressive phenotype of MDSCs, leading to profound T cell inhibition and tumor progression. We hypothesize that combinatorial therapeutic strategies—targeting lactate production, its transport or downstream lactylation (via pharmacological inhibitors or CRISPR‐mediated disruption of lactylation enzymes) alongside the blockade of the GM‑CSF/STAT3 axis—will disrupt these synergistic networks. Furthermore, state-of-the-art techniques such as single-cell RNA sequencing, single-cell epigenomic profiling, multiplex CRISPR screening, and in vivo lactate imaging will be employed to validate each causal step and refine the therapeutic window in cancer immunotherapies.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on the concept that tumor-derived lactate induces histone lactylation in MDSCs, leading to upregulation of ARG1 and iNOS and promoting immune evasion via T cell suppression, in parallel with GM‑CSF/STAT3 signaling. The revised hypothesis retains the core elements of the original causal chain—high glycolytic activity producing lactate, lactate uptake by MDSCs, lactate-induced histone lactylation, and consequent upregulation of immunosuppressive genes culminating in tumor progression. However, it expands the framework by: (1) acknowledging lactate’s additional impact on Treg stabilization through protein lactylation (e.g., MOESIN), (2) explicitly detailing the integration and potential synergy of the lactate-induced epigenetic mechanism with the GM‑CSF/STAT3 pathway, (3) emphasizing the use of contemporary technologies (such as single-cell RNA sequencing, single-cell epigenomic profiling, multiplex CRISPR screening, and in vivo lactate imaging) to validate each step, and (4) proposing a more robust combinatorial therapeutic strategy that targets multiple nodes in this cascade for improved clinical applicability.
